title: The Swollen Fox
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A hungry Fox found in a hollow tree a quantity of bread and meat, which some shepherds had placed there against their return. Delighted with his find he slipped in through the narrow aperture and greedily devoured it all.

But when he tried to get out again he found himself so swollen after his big meal that he could not squeeze through the hole, and fell to whining and groaning over his misfortune. Another Fox, happening to pass that way, came and asked him what the matter was; and, on learning the state of the case, said, "Well, my friend, I see nothing for it but for you to stay where you are till you shrink to your former size; you'll get out then easily enough."

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the hungry Fox find in the hollow tree?
options: A store of dried fruit
A hidden nest of eggs
A quantity of bread and meat
A pile of grain and corn

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who had placed the food in the tree?
options: Some shepherds, against their return
A group of travelling merchants
The Fox's own family
A farmer storing food for winter

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Fox get into the tree?
options: He digs a new hole at the base
He climbs in from the top of the tree
He is helped in by another fox
He slips in through the narrow aperture

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why can't the Fox get back out of the tree?
options: The hole has been blocked by falling branches
He is too swollen after his big meal to squeeze through the hole
He is too weak from hunger to climb out
The shepherds have returned and are blocking the exit

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who comes across the trapped Fox?
options: A curious shepherd
A passing wolf
Another Fox
A group of hunters

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what advice does the other Fox give?
options: To stay where he is until he shrinks to his former size
To break down the tree with his own strength
To call out for the shepherds to help him
To eat even more so he can push through the hole

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Fox end up trapped after such a satisfying meal?
options: The hole shrank in size while he was eating
The shepherds sealed the opening while he was inside
He was too full to remember which way was out
His greed led him to eat far more than the narrow opening could later allow him to pass through

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why is the other Fox's advice ultimately the only real solution?
options: The other Fox has a secret way to widen the hole
Only time and digestion, not effort, can undo the effect of overeating
The shepherds are expected to return and help free him
Whining loudly will eventually attract help from someone else

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "aperture" mean in "the narrow aperture"?
options: A type of tool
A hidden passage underground
An opening or gap
A large branch of a tree

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: Overindulging can trap you in the very situation your greed created
Foxes should never eat food left behind by shepherds
Asking for help is always more effective than waiting
Hollow trees make unsafe hiding places for any animal

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Fox do to the food once he finds it?
options: He saves some for later
He shares it with a passing Fox
He carries it away to a safer spot
He greedily devours it all

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the trapped Fox do while stuck in the tree?
options: He remains completely silent, hoping not to be noticed
He falls to whining and groaning over his misfortune
He tries repeatedly to break through the wood
He calls out for the shepherds to return quickly

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the second Fox address the trapped Fox?
options: "Poor fellow"
"Foolish one"
"My friend"
"Stranger"

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the second Fox seem calm rather than alarmed by the situation?
options: He recognizes the problem will resolve itself naturally over time
He does not believe the first Fox is truly trapped
He plans to free the Fox himself using tools
He is indifferent to what happens to the trapped Fox

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the trapped Fox's "misfortune" ultimately stem from?
options: The shepherds returning too early to catch him
The tree's hole being smaller than usual
Bad luck that had nothing to do with his own actions
His own choice to eat greedily rather than moderately

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "devoured" mean in "greedily devoured it all"?
options: Hid away carefully
Ate quickly and completely
Shared generously with others
Wasted or spilled

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Fox is freed immediately by another passing fox
A Fox shares his food with the shepherds who own it
A Fox eats so much that he becomes trapped, and is told he must simply wait to shrink back down
A Fox escapes the tree by digging a new hole
